title: Validate Binary Search Tree
directAnswer: A BST is valid only if EVERY node satisfies the global ordering — not just its immediate parent. The interview-grade answer is a DFS that passes down a (low, high) open interval: each node must be strictly inside its bounds, then recurse left with high = node.val and right with low = node.val. The elegant alternative is an inorder traversal, which must produce a strictly increasing sequence. Both are O(n) time, O(h) space.

remember.pattern: Bounds-propagating DFS (min/max interval) — or strictly-increasing inorder
remember.formula:
valid(node, low, high):
    if node is null: return True
    if not (low < node.val < high): return False
    return valid(node.left, low, node.val)
       and valid(node.right, node.val, high)
rules: Validity is **global**, not local — a node must beat *every* ancestor, not just its parent. This is THE trap of the problem.
Comparisons are **strict** (`<`, not `≤`) — BSTs here forbid duplicate values across the ordering.
Pass the bound *open interval* down: recurse left with `high = node.val`, recurse right with `low = node.val`.
Seed the root with `(-∞, +∞)`. Use `Long.MIN_VALUE/MAX_VALUE` or `null` sentinels to survive `Integer.MIN/MAX_VALUE` node values.
Inorder alternative: a valid BST's inorder traversal is **strictly increasing** — track the previous value and fail on `prev >= curr`.
whenToUse: You must verify a tree obeys the BST ordering invariant everywhere
Any 'is this tree a valid X?' where the constraint propagates from ancestors to descendants
You can exploit that inorder of a BST is sorted (validate, kth-smallest, fix-swapped-nodes)
antiSignals: You only compare each node to its direct parent → that's the buggy 'local check' that fails [5,4,6,null,null,3,7]
The tree isn't a BST at all → ordering reasoning doesn't apply
You need the values themselves sorted, not a yes/no → just do an inorder traversal
remember.takeaway: The whole problem is a trap about the word 'every'. Once you realize each node is constrained by an interval inherited from all its ancestors — not just its parent — the bounds-DFS writes itself. The inorder-is-sorted view is the same idea from a different angle and is worth knowing for the whole BST family.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you understand that the BST property is global. Many candidates write a check that only compares a node to its immediate children and pass the trivial cases while failing on deeper violations.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing only node.val against node.left.val and node.right.val (local check), and forgetting integer overflow when seeding bounds with Integer.MIN/MAX_VALUE.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the global-vs-local insight explicitly, handle the overflow with Long or null bounds, and offer the inorder-is-strictly-increasing alternative as a second solution.

problemStatement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, determine if it is a **valid binary search tree (BST)**.

A valid BST is defined as follows:

- The left subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys **strictly less** than the node's key.
- The right subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys **strictly greater** than the node's key.
- Both the left and right subtrees must also be binary search trees.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10⁴]
-2³¹ ≤ Node.val ≤ 2³¹ − 1 (values can equal Integer.MIN_VALUE / MAX_VALUE — beware overflow)
Duplicates are not allowed under the strict ordering
understanding: Return true only if the tree obeys the BST ordering at every node. The key subtlety: 'left subtree only contains smaller keys' applies to the entire subtree, so a deeply nested node can violate an ancestor's bound even while looking fine relative to its own parent.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are duplicate values allowed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Per the standard definition, no — comparisons are strict. If duplicates were allowed you'd relax one side to ≤, so confirm the rule before coding.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can node values be at the integer limits?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — values can equal Integer.MIN_VALUE or MAX_VALUE. That's why you seed bounds with Long or null sentinels rather than Integer.MIN/MAX.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is a single node a valid BST?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. The constraints guarantee at least one node, and a lone node trivially satisfies the ordering.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you want a yes/no, or the offending node?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: LeetCode wants a boolean. If they later ask to repair the tree (Recover BST), the inorder approach that finds the out-of-order pair becomes the better foundation.

examples.explanation: Left child 1 < 2 and right child 3 > 2. Every node is within its bounds.
Node 4 is in the right subtree of 5, so it must be > 5, but 4 < 5. The violation is against an ancestor, not the parent.
The classic trap: 3 is 6's left child (3 < 6 looks fine locally) but 3 lives in 5's right subtree, so it must be > 5. A local-only check wrongly passes this.

diagrams.title: Picking the right validation
diagrams.caption: Bounds-DFS is the default; inorder is the equally-good alternative that reuses 'BST inorder is sorted'.

approaches.name: Local-Only Check (Brute / Wrong — Name to Reject)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention briefly as the tempting-but-broken first idea, then reject it with a counterexample. It shows you anticipated the trap.
hints: The naïve reading is: each node just needs its left child smaller and right child larger. Why might that not be enough?
Construct [5,4,6,null,null,3,7]: every parent-child pair looks valid, yet 3 sits in 5's right subtree where everything must exceed 5.
The fix is to remember not just the parent but the tightest lower and upper bound inherited from ALL ancestors.
approaches.complexityReasoning: It still visits every node once (O(n)) with O(h) recursion depth, but correctness — not complexity — is the problem: it accepts invalid trees.
approaches.explanation:
The instinctive solution checks, at each node, only that `node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val`. It runs in linear time and passes shallow examples, which is exactly why it's dangerous.

**Why it's wrong.** The BST property says the *entire* left subtree is smaller and the *entire* right subtree is larger — a transitive, global constraint. A grandchild can satisfy its parent yet violate a grandparent. In `[5,4,6,null,null,3,7]`, node `3` is the left child of `6` (so `3 < 6` passes the local test), but `6` is in `5`'s right subtree, meaning every node under `6` — including `3` — must be greater than `5`. A local check never sees the bound inherited from `5`, so it wrongly returns true.

**The lesson.** The only safe information to carry is the *interval* `(low, high)` accumulated from every ancestor on the path down. Mentioning this broken approach and immediately refuting it with the counterexample is a strong signal you understand the problem's actual difficulty.
approaches.insight: The bug is conceptual, not syntactic — the code is clean and fast, it's just answering the wrong question. Interviewers plant exactly this trap, so the move that scores points is naming it before you fall into it.

dryRun.intro: We show why the local check passes a tree that is actually invalid.

steps.state: tree is INVALID → local check is wrong

dryRun.result: Local check says true; correct answer is false.

java.line: if (node.left != null && node.left.val >= node.val) return false;
java.explanation: Only checks the DIRECT left child — never the inherited ancestor bound, so it misses deep violations.
Recurses without passing any bound down — each subtree forgets its ancestors entirely.

python.explanation: Local-only comparison; blind to grandparent constraints.
No bounds threaded through the recursion — the core defect.

pitfalls: Believing this is correct because it passes [2,1,3] and other shallow trees.
Not testing against a deep-violation case like [5,4,6,null,null,3,7].
Shipping it because it's O(n) — speed is irrelevant when the answer is wrong.

approaches.name: Bounds-Propagating DFS (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'each node carries an open interval inherited from its ancestors'.
hints: What if every node knew the tightest lower and upper value it's allowed to take, based on the turns taken from the root?
Going LEFT tightens the upper bound to the parent's value; going RIGHT tightens the lower bound to the parent's value. Seed the root with (-∞, +∞).
At each node assert low < node.val < high. If it holds, recurse left with (low, node.val) and right with (node.val, high). Use Long or null sentinels to dodge integer overflow at the limits.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is checked once against its O(1) bounds → O(n) time. Recursion depth equals the height h → O(h) space, which is O(log n) for a balanced tree and O(n) worst case for a skewed tree.
approaches.explanation:
Thread an open interval `(low, high)` through the recursion that captures the constraint inherited from every ancestor on the path to the current node. A node is valid iff `low < node.val < high`.

**How the interval evolves.** Start the root with `(-∞, +∞)` — it may be any value. When you descend into the **left** child, that whole subtree must be less than the current node, so the upper bound tightens to `node.val`: recurse with `(low, node.val)`. When you descend into the **right** child, everything must exceed the current node, so the lower bound tightens to `node.val`: recurse with `(node.val, high)`. The bounds only ever get narrower as you go deeper, which is precisely how the global constraint is enforced locally.

**Why this fixes the trap.** Re-run `[5,4,6,null,null,3,7]`. Root 5 has bounds `(-∞,+∞)`. Going right to 6 gives bounds `(5, +∞)`. Going left from 6 to 3 gives bounds `(5, 6)`. Now `3` is checked against `5 < 3 < 6`, which is false — caught immediately. The bound `5` survived two levels down because we *carried it*, which the local check never did.

**The overflow detail.** Node values can be exactly `Integer.MIN_VALUE` or `MAX_VALUE`. If you seed bounds with those same ints and compare with strict `<`, a legitimate extreme value gets rejected, or arithmetic on the bound overflows. The clean fixes are to type the bounds as `Long` (`Long.MIN_VALUE/MAX_VALUE`) or to use `null` to mean 'no bound yet' and skip the comparison when a bound is null. Mention this proactively — it's the detail that separates a correct answer from one that fails a hidden test.
approaches.insight: The mental model is a shrinking window. Every left turn lowers the ceiling, every right turn raises the floor, and the window can only narrow. A node is valid exactly when it lands strictly inside the window it inherited — that single sentence is the whole algorithm.

dryRun.intro: Bounds shown as (low, high), open interval. The root starts unconstrained.

java.explanation: Seed with Long bounds — using Integer.MIN/MAX would wrongly reject valid nodes at the int limits.

java.line: if (node.val <= low || node.val >= high) return false;
java.explanation: Strict containment: a node must be STRICTLY inside its inherited open interval.
Descending left tightens the upper bound to the current value.
Descending right raises the lower bound to the current value.

python.explanation: Python chained comparison expresses the strict open-interval check directly.
Left child inherits the same floor but a ceiling of node.val.
Right child inherits a floor of node.val and the same ceiling.
float infinities sidestep overflow entirely — no value can equal ±inf.

edgeCases.behavior: With Long/inf bounds it passes; with Integer.MIN_VALUE seeds and a <= check it would wrongly fail. This is the overflow test.
Duplicate values violate strict ordering — 2 is not < 2, so it returns false.

pitfalls: Seeding with Integer.MIN_VALUE/MAX_VALUE — breaks on nodes holding those exact values.
Using <= / >= where strict < / > is required (or vice versa) — flips the duplicate-handling behaviour.
Swapping which bound tightens on left vs right — a very common copy-paste slip.

approaches.name: Inorder Traversal — Strictly Increasing (Alternative)
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as a clean second solution and the natural lead-in to Kth Smallest / Recover BST. Emphasize the 'inorder of a BST is sorted' invariant.
hints: Recall what an inorder traversal of a BST produces. If the tree is valid, what property must that output sequence have?
Inorder of a valid BST is strictly increasing. So do an inorder walk and compare each value to the previous one.
Keep a single `prev` variable. The instant you see prev >= current, the tree is invalid — you can bail early without finishing the walk.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single inorder pass touches every node once → O(n). Done recursively the call stack is O(h); the iterative-stack version is also O(h). You only store one previous value, so no extra O(n) buffer is needed.
approaches.explanation:
This approach leans on the defining property of BSTs: an **inorder traversal visits values in sorted order if and only if the tree is a valid BST**. So instead of reasoning about bounds, just walk the tree inorder and confirm the output is strictly increasing.

**The mechanism.** Carry a single `prev` value (initially negative infinity / null). Each time the inorder walk reaches a node, compare `node.val` with `prev`. If `node.val <= prev`, the sequence isn't strictly increasing, so the tree is invalid — return false immediately. Otherwise update `prev = node.val` and continue. Because we only ever look at adjacent elements of the inorder sequence, one scalar of state is enough; we don't materialize the whole sorted list.

**Why it's equivalent to the bounds version.** Both enforce the global ordering — the bounds version does it spatially (an interval per node) while the inorder version does it temporally (the just-visited value is the strictest lower bound for the next value). They have identical O(n)/O(h) cost; pick whichever you can write more confidently. The inorder framing also generalizes beautifully: stop at the kth node for Kth Smallest, or record the two out-of-order nodes for Recover Binary Search Tree.
approaches.insight: If you remember exactly one fact about BSTs for interviews, make it 'inorder traversal yields sorted order'. It turns Validate BST, Kth Smallest, BST Iterator, and Recover BST all into variations on a single inorder walk.

dryRun.intro: Inorder visits left, node, right. prev starts at -∞. Fail the moment values stop strictly increasing.

steps.action: 3 > 5? NO (3 came from 4's left in the right subtree)

java.explanation: Validate the entire left subtree first — that's the 'left' half of inorder.

java.line: if (prev != null && prev.val >= node.val) return false;
java.explanation: The just-visited value must be strictly smaller; >= means the sorted invariant broke.
Advance the running 'previous in sorted order' pointer.
Continue into the right subtree to check the rest of the sequence.

python.explanation: Short-circuit: if the left subtree already failed, stop.
Strictly-increasing test against the previous inorder value.
Update the previous value before descending right.
Recurse right to validate the remainder of the inorder sequence.

edgeCases.behavior: Inorder yields 1,1 — not strictly increasing, so returns false (duplicates rejected).
Using a null/-inf prev avoids overflow; sequence MIN, MAX is increasing → true.

pitfalls: Initializing prev to Integer.MIN_VALUE — a node equal to MIN_VALUE then fails the >= test incorrectly; use null or -inf.
Using >= vs > inconsistently with the duplicate rule.
Collecting the full inorder list then checking sortedness — works but wastes O(n) memory; one prev variable suffices.

commonMistakes: Doing a local-only check (node vs its direct children) and missing ancestor violations.
Seeding bounds with Integer.MIN_VALUE/MAX_VALUE and failing on nodes holding those exact values.
Using non-strict comparisons (<=, >=) and accidentally accepting duplicate values.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Local comparison instead of inherited bounds
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Checking node.val only against its immediate children passes [5,4,6,null,null,3,7] even though 3 violates the ancestor bound from 5. Validity is global.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Integer overflow on the seed bounds
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Seeding with Integer.MIN_VALUE/MAX_VALUE breaks when a node holds exactly that value, because the strict comparison then rejects a legitimate node. Use Long or null.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong strictness lets duplicates through
commonMistakesDetailed.why: BSTs here forbid equal keys. Using < where the bound check should reject equality (or vice versa) silently accepts an invalid duplicate.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: if (node.val < low || node.val > high) return false;  // allows node.val == bound
commonMistakesDetailed.good: if (node.val <= low || node.val >= high) return false; // strictly inside only

followupVariations.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
followupVariations.hint: Inorder traversal is sorted — return the kth value emitted, stopping early.

followupVariations.title: Recover Binary Search Tree
followupVariations.hint: Inorder finds the two nodes that are out of strictly-increasing order; swap their values.

followupVariations.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST
followupVariations.hint: Use the BST ordering to decide which subtree to descend — no full search needed.

followupVariations.title: Search in a Binary Search Tree
followupVariations.hint: The same ordering invariant lets you binary-search the tree in O(h).

patternNote: Bounds-propagating DFS enforces a global invariant by carrying ancestor information down the recursion as a shrinking interval. The inorder-is-sorted view is the BST-specific twin. This pair of ideas underpins the entire BST family: Kth Smallest, Recover BST, LCA of a BST, and BST iterators.
